## Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

### Traditional image of toughness
When college students were asked to describe toughness, words like hard-nosed, gritty, playing through pain, stoic, exhibiting emotional fortitude, showing no signs of distress, persevering came to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance came out on top. The image that arises is a football player popping his dislocated shoulder back in, Craig MacTavish who retired in 1997 as the last player in the NHL to play without a helmet, a wounded military hero or a mother fighting through discomfort. Toughness is traditionally viewed as overcoming obstacles with perseverance, discipline and stoicism, and many picture a strong brute of a man.

### Bobby Knight and the authoritarian model
Bobby Knight’s career spanned five decades and three universities. He won more than nine hundred games, the third most all-time in college basketball; reached the Final Four five times; and took home three NCAA national championships. His 1976 Indiana team won every game they played, sweeping through the NCAA tournament with a win over Michigan to seal the perfect season and Knight’s first national championship. No team has matched their record since.

Knight described what set them apart: “That was a team that was almost impossible to beat, because of its toughness, its strength, its size.” For a man who began at West Point, toughness seemed easy to define: “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” The team pioneered a pressing man-to-man defense that tested discipline, work ethic and perseverance.

Knight’s methods are abusive. There were tampons hanging from lockers of players he thought were “soft.” Frequent cussing out of players and accusation he ordered managers to tape pictures of women’s genitalia in players’ rooms. The 1991 tape: “This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I’ll fucking run your ass right into the ground. . . . I had to sit around for a fucking year with an 8–10 record in this fucking league, and I mean you will not put me in that fucking position again or you will goddamn pay for it like you can’t fucking believe.” He brought a piece of toilet paper covered in shit to show players what he thought of them. Physical abuse marked by video of Knight choking a player at practice.

“Soft.” Female genitalia. Questioning manhood. All clue us in on Knight’s actual definition of toughness, founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing through obstacles, and utilizing fear to establish authority and control. A version now called old-school. It still dominates playing fields.

### Tough parenting and demand-support mismatch
In the 1960s, developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind pioneered understanding of parenting. Styles are classified by responsiveness and demandingness. Responsiveness is “the extent to which parents intentionally foster individuality, self-regulation, and self-assertion by being attuned, supportive, and acquiescent to children’s special needs and demands.” Demandingness refers to “the claims parents make on children to become integrated into the family whole, by their maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts and willingness to confront the child who disobeys.”

Low demandingness and high responsiveness is permissive. High demandingness and low responsiveness is authoritarian, relying on harsh discipline with little attention to child’s needs. Authoritarian parents don’t trust children to make good decisions. A typical refrain is, “You need to do (this) because I said so.” In one study of over one thousand parents, only 31 percent of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally.”

Authoritarian parents jump straight to criticism after a missed shot, ground a kid after every subpar test score, or command boys to suck it up, don’t cry, grow up, and never show fear. In one study, 81 percent of Americans thought parents were too soft on their children. Many see harsh discipline as beneficial and lack of it as sign of “softening” of America.

Punishment or telling a child to simply “work harder” doesn’t always get results, and when demandingness far outweighs support, problems arise. The “just right” fit is high demand accompanied by warmth and understanding.

### Callousness, machismo and fake toughness
Callous: to harden, to make insensitive, to develop a thick skin. Language around toughness proclaims teams “soft,” in need of “hardening up,” and implores teams to “show no signs of weakness.” In youth sports, kids run laps or perform burpees to “toughen them up.” In Until It Hurts, Mark Hyman visited youth sport clubs across the country and found frequent throwing up after workouts, insult-laden tirades, and more. The justification parents provided for teaching eleven-year-olds to go until they puke? “The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.”

Toughness has been tied to masculinity and machismo. We tell sons and daughters to “man up” or “stop being a pussy.” As A League of Their Own summarized, “There’s no crying in baseball!”

The old model is Bobby Knight school of coaching, authoritarian parents, and callous model of leading. It’s myth of an “inner warrior,” built on callous demandingness. Toughness has been hijacked. External displays are prioritized over true inner strength.

### Downfall of a callous view
On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football team had ten 110-yard sprints for conditioning. By number seven, nineteen-year-old Jordan McNair began to show profound fatigue, bending over at waist and experiencing cramps. Instead of pulling him, coaches and athletic trainers goaded him, yelling to “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” By final sprint, video shows McNair surrounded by teammates aiding him at near-walking pace. After McNair complained of cramps, it took trainers 34 minutes to have him taken off field and another 28 minutes to call 911. One hour and 28 minutes elapsed between final sprint and ambulance. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke, thanks in part to horrid medical response but also to inability to separate pushing through pain and actual danger.

Rhabdomyolysis, or rhabdo, is once-rare condition where damaged muscle products leak into bloodstream, putting unusual demand on kidneys. A disease once primarily caused by infections or drug use has transformed into somewhat common occurrence from extreme workouts. As professor B. David Ridpath described, true notion of these workouts is not conditioning: “Taking a cue from a head coach with a desire to either toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots, the strength coach often will ‘condition’ these players with a vengeance and a mandate to make them suffer.”

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggressive behavior, and higher likelihood for substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, controlling style is linked to lower grit and increase in emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to much higher rate of child misbehavior. In Israeli military, those who grew up in authoritarian environment adapted to and coped with military life much worse than peers who grew up in nurturing environment.

Teaching for this version of toughness creates fragile and dependent individuals. One young athlete said: “Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger. . . . It gets in your head and you start thinking, ‘I need to do better. I need to work harder because I don’t want to be punished.’” He wanted to avoid punishment, not get better.

### Redefining toughness
In trying to toughen through callousness, we’ve trained ourselves to respond to fear and power. Remove fear, power and control, and the “tough” individual is left without skills to navigate adversity. The old view gives him a hammer and expects him to bash through any problem.

Fake toughness is easy to identify. It’s Bobby Knight losing control and throwing tantrums in name of “discipline.” It’s appearance of power without substance. It’s control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and based on appearance over substance.

Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make best decision you can. Research shows this model is more effective than old one.

Pete Carroll isn’t a saint; he’s a coach. After losing job as NFL head coach in 1990s, Carroll stopped imitating others and followed own path. He allows players to be who they are, celebrates “the way they see the world,” encourages meditation and yoga or shifts from meeting to playing ring toss if players get heated. According to one star player, “He’s never negative, doesn’t scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive.” Carroll is one of only three coaches in history to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl.

Carroll wants players who come through when game is on line. He believes toughness comes from inner drive to keep them focused, from embracing challenges and bouncing back, from perseverance and passion. “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do and believing what they can do and they go out there and do it,” Carroll relayed to The Bleacher Report.

Consider Don Shula, Bill Walsh, and Tony Dungy, among most successful coaches in NFL history. In basketball, consider John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, or Mike D’Antoni, who said, “We keep it positive here.” As Ken Reed summarized, “For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach. . . . Despite the success of Wooden, Shula, Dungy, Stevens, and others, our society has conditioned us to think that autocratic coaches are better coaches; that they win more often. It’s a myth. But it’s a vicious cycle.”

In 2008, researchers out of Eastern Washington explored relationship between leadership style and development of toughness. After research on nearly two hundred basketball players and coaches, they concluded, “The results of this study seem to suggest that the ‘keys’ to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach’s ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service.”

Real toughness is providing tool set to handle adversity. It’s teaching. Fake toughness creates fragility, responding out of fear, suppressing what we feel, and attempting to press onward no matter situation. Real toughness pushes us to work with body and mind instead of against them. Toughness is having space to make right choice under discomfort.

TOUGHNESS MAXIM
Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.

### Searching for real toughness
The author recounts Don Bowden Mile. In 1957, Bowden, twenty-year-old Cal economics student, became first American to break mythical four-minute-mile barrier. Fifty years later, seven men lined up to chase same feat. Six wore blue and gold of University of California, Berkeley, and author wore red and white of University of Houston.

At 900 meters into 1,609-meter race, sensation in neck of tightening and straining appeared, with strange high-pitched gasp. Mind jumped into action: “What was that? What’s wrong? Why am I breathing hard? This is too soon. My legs feel fine. You’re done.” After freak-out, author put head down and tried to grind through. Less than 100 meters later, inner voice screamed, “I can’t breathe. What the hell!? I can’t breathe!” He pulled off, collapsed onto knees, and after panic-stricken moments blockage cleared.

For next year, tests ranging from scopes to echocardiograms to treadmill tests were done. Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction, VCD. Vocal cords sit in larynx and open widely when breathing in and partially close when breathing out. With VCD, flaps malfunction, shutting when they are supposed to open, blocking airways on inhalation. Current theory is vocal cords become hyperresponsive. American Thoracic Society cites “strong emotions” and stress as triggers.

Activity that defined author’s sense of self-worth transformed into something feared. To continue, he had to relax, keep breathing, neck and mind steady at exact moment discomfort and doubts were highest. Book started moment he collapsed, search for what it means to be tough.

Running serves as central thread because it is sport where you are alone, in your head, navigating immense discomfort. Lessons apply far beyond sport to parenting, grief, managing and leading people.

Four pillars of real toughness are introduced:
* PILLAR 1: Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
* PILLAR 2: Listen to Your Body
* PILLAR 3: Respond Instead of React
* PILLAR 4: Transcend Discomfort

Chapter closes by noting fundamental misunderstanding of toughness. Being tough is attainable to all. Most walk around with wrong framework, stuck in old-school mindset. Real toughness isn’t just about helping you deal with pain or perform better; it’s about making you healthier, happier human being.
